nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_000
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What percentage of global GHG emissions was attributed to the combined manufacturing, energy, transport, and building sectors in 2019?
nodes.paragraph: In 2019, the combined manufacturing, energy, transport, and building sectors were responsible for approximately 79% of the global GHG emissions, whereas agriculture, forestry, and land use accounted for 22%7. Energy economics research has identified energy consumption and economic growth as the foremost contributors to environmental conditions10,11,15,16. Grossman and Krueger1 17 hypothesised an inverted U-shaped link between real growth and ecological deterioration. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis, named after Kuznets18. Numerous studies have validated the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis, indicating that economies heavily reliant on fossil fuels often experience environmental degradation in the early stages of development. At a certain threshold level, adopting better technologies may enhance environmental quality1,5 The impact of trade openness on economic growth and environmental sustainability has recently become a prominent subject of academic research19,20 Trade liberalisation accelerates economic growth and affects pollution levels by allowing countries to leverage their comparative advantages through resource transfer10. Trade openness enhances energy usage through industrial exports and imports of goods, such as automobiles and industrial inputs5,14.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_001
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What role does precision engineering play in reducing emissions?
nodes.answer: Avoiding overdesign through precision engineering contributes to emissions reductions.
nodes.paragraph: By replacing fossil fuel-based thermal energy with electricity from renewable sources the cement industry can significantly reduce its carbon footprint while energy effi - ciency and supporting the global transition to sustainable energy systems [ 9]. In the construction phase, optimizing concrete mixes to meet specific project needs, utilizing renewable energy sources, and incorporating recycled materials can signifi - cantly cut emissions [ 10, 11]. Avoiding overdesign through precision engineering, leveraging just-in-time deliveries, and embracing advanced construction technologies also contrib - ute to emissions reductions [ 12]. Educating the design and construction community to prioritize performance-based specifications fosters innovation in sustainable cement and concrete solutions, enhancing structural performance, energy efficiency, and resilience, while enabling carbon sequestration. In the long term, energy-efficient buildings constructed with low-carbon cement would reduce opera - tional emissions, while concrete S durability would reduce the need for frequent maintenance, extending infrastruc - ture lifespans and lowering associated emissions. Concrete, while highly recyclable, may not be 100% recyclable in all cases due to factors such as contamination, material degra - dation, and the limitations of current recycling technologies.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_002
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What relationship between temperature and total factor productivity (TFP) was found in Chinese manufacturing plants according to Zhang et al. (2018)?
nodes.answer: An inverted U-shape relationship between temperature and TFP was found.
nodes.paragraph: We find that under a middle-of-the-road climate projection of the period 2020 2039, annual global trade is reduced by about 735 million USD due to additional high temperature events relative to 2015. 1.1 Literature Review Growing micro- and plant-level evidence suggests that high ambient temperature has det - rimental impacts on labour productivity and supply. Using survey data on time allocation of individuals, Zivin and Neidell ( 2014 ) find evidence for a substantial reduction of labour supply in climate-exposed industries such as agriculture, construction and manufacturing in non-climate-controlled facilities on days with maximum temperature above 85 F (29.4 C). Given the evidence on the temperature-productivity relationship of individuals, one might suggest that such temperature effects prevail also on plant-level. Looking at the near- universe of Chinese manufacturing plants from 1998 to 2007, Zhang et al. (2018 ) find an inverted U-shape relationship between temperature and total factor productivity (TFP). Their estimates show that for the average plant on a day with maximum temperature above 90 F (32.24 C), TFP decreases by 0.56 percent relative to a day with 50 60 F (10 15 C), translating into an estimated output loss of 0.45 percent for the average plant.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_003
nodes.question: What approach does the interviewee believe is more effective in influencing employees to reduce CO2 emissions - top-down or bottom-up?
nodes.answer: The interviewee believes that the bottom-up approach, focusing on the employee and providing positive incentives for good behaviour, is more effective in influencing employees to reduce CO2 emissions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_004
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What measures does the dress manufacturer take to reduce emissions and lower their emission cost?
nodes.answer: The dress manufacturer installs solar panels and wind turbines with green technology investment to reduce emissions and lower their emission cost.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_005
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How does the textile industry aim to reduce emissions at the supplier stage, and what technologies are being invested in?
nodes.answer: The textile industry is investing in green technologies such as solar panels and wind turbines to reduce emissions at the supplier stage. These investments are aimed at lowering the amount of greenhouse gases emitted during manufacturing processes.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_006
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: How can rental platforms reduce greenhouse gas emissions per product compared to owning, according to the comparative LCA results?
nodes.answer: Rental platforms can reduce greenhouse gas emissions per product if the number of wears increases from owned to rented and the use of dry cleaning is minimized.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_007
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How did the GHG emissions reduce significantly from owning to renting with maxi dresses?
nodes.answer: The GHG emissions reduced significantly from owning to renting with maxi dresses because formal wear like maxi dresses have higher GHG emissions during production and can be worn more frequently when rented, leading to a decrease in overall emissions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_008
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How can rental platforms reduce greenhouse gas emissions per piece and per product?
nodes.answer: Rental platforms can reduce greenhouse gas emissions per piece and per product by increasing the number of wears from owned to rented items and minimizing the use of dry cleaning.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_009
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What percentage of emissions in the textile industry is associated with materials manufacture?
nodes.answer: The largest part of emissions in the textile industry (approximately 40%) is associated with materials manufacture.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_010
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: What percentage of textiles' total climate change impact occurs in the production phase?
nodes.answer: About 80% of textiles' total climate change impact occurs in the production phase.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_011
nodes.label: Science and Tech
nodes.question: What percentage of global greenhouse gas emissions is contributed by textile production, as emphasized by Costa et al. (2018)?
nodes.answer: According to Costa et al. (2018), textile production contributes to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions, primarily due to energy-intensive manufacturing processes.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_012
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How does the manufacturing process of nylon fabric contribute to global warming?
nodes.answer: The manufacturing of nylon fabric is energy-intensive, consuming three times more energy than cotton. This production process releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas that is more harmful than carbon dioxide in depleting the ozone layer.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Carbon footprint reduction|Low-carbon manufacturing processes_qna_013
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What changes were observed in greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, water use, and land use over time in participants of different textiles?
nodes.answer: Participants in T1 had significantly higher reductions in GHGs and energy consumption compared to T2 and T3, while their water use increased more. Land use did not show a significant difference.
